quote: Wahrscheinlich kann man nach meiner obigen Methode der inneren Unverzweigtheit auch die Differentialgl. für $C(x)$, $A(x)y$, $B(x)z$ aufstellen.
english: Probably one can also set up, by my above method of inner unramifiedness, the differential equations for $C(x)$, $A(x)y$, $B(x)z$.
topic: Notes on using continued fraction (and ternary chain-algorithm) expansions of the error-type function $e^{x^2}\int_0^x e^{-t^2}dt$ together with $e^{-x^2}$ to prove irrationality results, via differential equations, recursion formulas and generating functions.

triage.modern_statement: Take y(x) = e^{x^2}∫_0^x e^{-t^2}dt, which is the Dawson-type function e^{x^2}·(√π/2)·erf(x), and z(x) = e^{-x^2}. Build the type-I Hermite–Padé (simultaneous rational) approximation in which polynomials A_n, B_n, C_n make the remainder A_n(x)y + B_n(x)z + C_n(x) vanish to high order at x = 0. These come from a ternary, Jacobi–Perron-type chain algorithm generalizing continued fractions. Hilbert's question is whether the polynomials C(x), and the products A(x)y and B(x)z, satisfy explicit linear differential equations with polynomial coefficients in x, derived by his method of 'inner unramifiedness'. Such equations, together with recursions and generating functions, would then feed into proofs of irrationality or linear independence for the values.
triage.answered_by: Not attributable to one person or date. The general fact Hilbert expected became standard in the later theory of Hermite–Padé approximation for solutions of linear ODEs. Main contributors include K. Mahler, who developed Hermite's formulas, G. V. Chudnovsky around 1979–1980 (Padé approximations to solutions of linear differential equations and monodromy), and later work on semiclassical functions (e.g. arXiv:1502.01202, 2015). I found no source that addresses Hilbert's note itself, or this exact pair of functions, as a problem.

evidence.claim: Shows that Hermite–Padé polynomials for a vector of semiclassical functions can be associated with a linear differential equation with polynomial coefficients. A fundamental system of solutions of that equation is built from the approximants and remainders, which is the kind of result Hilbert expected.

G. V. Chudnovsky, 'Rational and Padé approximations to solutions of linear differential equations and the monodromy theory' (Lecture Notes in Physics 126, Les Houches 1979). This is a foundational treatment of Padé and Hermite–Padé approximants to solutions of linear ODEs and their use in number theory.
A 2022 arXiv paper studies linear and nonlinear (integrable) equations satisfied by Hermite–Padé polynomials and remainders, so the subject is still being worked on.
Recent work on algebraic properties of Hermite–Padé polynomials cites Chudnovsky's theory of approximations to solutions of linear differential equations.

triage.why: The note is a short methodological guess, not a precisely stated theorem. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Its content is a general principle: Hermite–Padé (simultaneous) approximants and remainders for functions satisfying linear ODEs, such as e^{x^2}∫e^{-t^2} and e^{-x^2}, themselves satisfy linear ODEs, recursions and closed generating functions. This principle was established later in the literature cited above and is still studied. The irrationality results it was meant to serve are classical: e^{r^2} is irrational for rational r ≠ 0 (since e^q is irrational for rational q ≠ 0, by Lambert and Hermite), and erf values are covered by Siegel–Shidlovskii E-function theory. I am basing that on general knowledge; my searches did not return a source for it. I could not find any source that discusses Hilbert's specific 'inner unramifiedness' method or this notebook entry, so linking it to the later results is my reading. That is why confidence is low.
